9-foot-tall Game Boy Color plays all the classics

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1438 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • According to recent reports, A pair of California-based engineers have built what they say may be the largest Game Boy Color ever.
  • The console has already appeared at several maker events, where eager kids have punched and kicked its chunky buttons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›.

According to recent reports, A pair of California-based engineers have built what they say may be the largest Game Boy Color ever. Standing more than nine feet and weighing around 300 pounds, the Pokémon-yellow goliath requires a U-Haul to transport and took over 1,500 collective hours in a makerspace to create. And it isn’t just for show. The giant handheld plays real Game Boy games, thanks to a pixel-perfect display scaled up from the original and software written from scratch. The designers even fabricated an assortment of to-scale accessories, including game cartridges, a cable link, and AA batteries.

The console has already appeared at several maker events, where eager kids have punched and kicked its chunky buttons. It has also prompted plenty of older millennials, in person and online, to reminisce about simpler days. Build videos posted across social media have racked up hundreds of thousands of views. But for co-creator Paige Powell, a veteran prop designer and mechanical engineer, the giant Game Boy also represents something more special: a labor of love and a chance to inspire young girls to start building things themselves.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​.

Recent findings suggest that “It [has] felt very weird to me in a very male-dominated world to build something behind the scenes and then give it to [a] guy who then takes credit,” Powell tells Popular Science. “I want people to see women making stuff!”.

The giant GameBoy is the joint effort of Powell (@whats_paige_making on Instagram) and engineer Nick Alvarez (@nickbuildstuff on Instagram). Powell has a long track record of building props and sets for the YouTube channel Mega Builds and the immersive art company Meow Wolf. Alvarez, meanwhile, specializes in PCB (printed circuit board) design and spent seven years as a full-time engineering manager at an aerospace defense company.

The two crossed paths while working at the Davis makerspace, just west of Sacramento. Alvarez was building a large LED wall (the kind used for screens at sports arenas) and wanted to hook up Nintendo controllers so it could play games. Piggybacking off of that, Powell proposed taking the idea a step further: a giant playable Game Boy. From there, it only made sense to try and make the world’s largest. That sent them down a rabbit hole that would consume a sizable chunk of their lives (and finances) over the months to follow.

It has been revealed that A quick bit of research revealed they weren’t the first one with this idea. Guinness World Records actually has an official entry for the Largest Game Boy Color, an accolade claimed in 2022 by a YouTuber named Jake Carlini. His version measured in at seven feet tall. But calling that one a real Game Boy is quite a stretch. It was really little more than a few pieces of vaguely detailed plywood. Alvarez and Powell realized there was an opportunity, not just to break the record, but to build something far more ambitious.

According to recent reports, “It [the Carlini model] was just kind of [a] slapstick way of putting it together, and we were like, ‘dude, what is this?’ Alvarez says. ”We can do something actually amazing with our background and our skillset.”.

From the outset, the duo gave themselves a set of constraints to build around. Their Game Boy had to be to scale to the original and functional as a game console. They also committed to making the screen pixel perfect to the 1998 original.

“Everything was built around the constraint of what the screen was going to be,” Powell claims.

Fortunately, they had some help along the way. When they told Tim Keller, the head of the Davis makerspace, about the project, he agreed to let them set up shop and use the space’s CNC mills, 3D printers, laser cutters, and other equipment.

Meet the college student crafting electric guitars from scratch.

This guy crammed a laptop into an Altoids tin.

Clever kid builds phone charger powered by pet hamster.

Teen brothers build a Disney-inspired ride in family basement.

Teen turns his suburban home into elaborate haunted house every October.

In Vermont, one man is bringing pay phones back to life.

With goals set and tools secured, the pair then created a 3D model of their scaled-up Game Boy, starting with a smaller (though still shockingly large) 5.7-foot version. Powell quickly realized that the toughest part to fabricate wasn’t actually the console’s iconic front, but rather its geometrically odd-shaped back shell. The top of the backside starts out flat but then bulges out into a sloped shape toward the bottom where a person would hold it in their palm. The cartridge slot where the game slides into also juts out from the back, adding even more complexity.

According to recent reports, once the 3D model was complete, Powell began building the physical body, made mostly of plywood shaped on the CNC machine, an automated manufacturing device that reads computer code and uses that to control cutting machines like mills, lathes, and lasers. CNC machines are indispensable tools in many makers’ arsenals. But a project like this requires adaptability. Partway through, Powell claims, she realized the CNC machine wasn’t all that well suited to making square cuts, which meant the final product would need more hand carpentry than initially planned.

Meanwhile, Alvarez was hard at work perfecting the display and electronics under the hood (or, in this case, the shell). He built the screen from a series of HUB75 LED panels, the kind commonly used in large digital signs. The trick was getting his massive DIY display to scale up accurately from the original GameBoy’s 160-by-144 pixel screen. He also used a small microcontroller (essentially a tiny computer assigned to a specific task) to map all of the device’s buttons and switches.

When the giant Game Boy plays games, it’s running them on a specialized emulator rather than the physical game cartridge that gets slotted into the device. The emulator is a piece of software that imitates a Game Boy. Emulators are common these days and are what let hobbyists play old Nintendo games on smartphones.

In a recent development, the to-scale cartridges Powell and Alvarez fabricated are really more for show. That means, theoretically, their device can run any Game Boy game. Alvarez says he even built in a feature that cycles to a different game each time the power is switched on. So far, the pair have posted videos of the device playing Pokémon and Donkey Kong. Alvarez even watched The Odyssey on it.

Powell and Alvarez have shown off their creations at two events so far: Open Sauce in 2026 and the Bay Area Maker Fair in Vallejo, California. Getting the Game Boys there was a task in itself. The larger of the two (around 300 pounds) required a large U-Haul and four people just to load it. Once unloaded, they faced a more daunting challenge: the wrath of children. Drawn in by the device’s giant buttons, kids at the events let loose.

“Kids were coming up and karate-kicking them, and I was just like, ‘Oh my God, man,’” Powell says.

Alvarez concurs. “They were punching the crap out of the buttons.”.

In a testament to its build quality, the giant Game Boy withstood the onslaught of toddler haymakers. Those who weren’t assailing the device were often absorbing an emotional gut punch of their own. Both in person and online, fans told Powell and Alvarez how the build brought back childhood memories. One commenter recalled how seeing it reminded them of a time at a school when a bully stole their beloved Game Boy. Decades later, he said, he’s still mad.

Looking ahead, Powell and Alvarez hope to find their creation a latest home where it can be on display and accessible to the public. They’d like to recoup some of the money they’ve poured into it, but Powell also expressed some wariness of it winding up locked away in some buyer’s private collection. Ideally, she states, it would land in a museum of some kind, where it could inspire the next generation of budding makers.

Recent findings suggest that in The Workshop, Popular Science highlights the ingenious, delightful, and often surprising projects people build in their spare time. If you or someone you know is working on a hobbyist project that fits the bill, we’d love to hear about it—fill out this form to tell us more.

#5931. Fera Fruit Oil Claims It’s Healthier Than Even Avocado Oil. Should You Make the Switch?

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1078 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Menshealth ↗ Open Full Page

Fera Fruit Oil Claims It’s Healthier Than Even Avocado Oil. Should You Make the Switch?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that EREWHON, EVERYONE’S FAVORITE love-to-hate overpriced supermarket chain made news recently for switching up their oils.
  • It has been revealed that erewhon isn’t the only organization hawking fera fruit oil as a way to further health-ify their vegan buffalo cauliflower and turmeric chicken tenders.
  • In a recent development, fera fruit oil may sound exotic and healthy (it’s made from fruit?), but as a registered dietitian, I'm not one for assumptions when it comes to food.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that EREWHON, EVERYONE’S FAVORITE love-to-hate overpriced supermarket chain made news recently for switching up their oils. Yes, the certified organic grocer announced that it's no longer using avocado oil to fry its cafe food. Instead, all 15 locations are switching to certified organic fera fruit oil.

It has been revealed that erewhon isn’t the only organization hawking fera fruit oil as a way to further health-ify their vegan buffalo cauliflower and turmeric chicken tenders. Since launching in April 2026, the oil is now in more than 800 grocers, restaurants, wellness clubs, and luxury hotels like Mezeh Mediterranean Grill and Wynn Las Vegas.

In a recent development, fera fruit oil may sound exotic and healthy (it’s made from fruit?), but as a registered dietitian, I'm not one for assumptions when it comes to food. Especially when it coincides with the peak of seed-oil fear-messaging. Keep reading to learn what this new-to-the-scene frying oil is and if it's really worth the hype.

FERA FRUIT OIL is basically palm oil. The company behind it, Zero Acre Farms, trademarked the name “fera fruit oil” for high oleic palm oil, a type of palm oil that's produced by pressing the fruit of a hybrid palm tree called Oleifera × Guineensis (OxG for short).

The hybrid plant was originally planted by farmers to reduce bud rot, a disease that notoriously destroys palm crops. A happy side effect was that the oil also ended up having higher oleic acid content, the same heart-healthy monounsaturated fat found in avocado and olive oil.

TRADITIONALLY GROWN PALM has a problematic history of deforestation, but according to Zero Acre Farms, fera fruit oil is a perennial crop that requires just 0.3 acres to produce a ton of oil, using 15 to 20 times less land than soybean or canola oil.

According to recent reports, of course, Zero Acre Farms’ website doesn't cite sources for these numbers, so I did my own digging. Independent research suggests traditional palm yields 3.3 tons per hectare, which is impressive compared to soybean, canola, and sunflower, which collectively produce 0.6 tons per hectare. But OxG palm yields about 1 ton less than traditional palm, which means the demonized seed oils use 3 to 4 times more land, not 15 to 20 times. So the claims seem a bit sensationalized at best?

COMPARED WITH REGULAR palm oil, high oleic palm oil—including the trademarked fera fruit oil—offers a significant nutritional upgrade.

According to recent reports, traditional palm oil contains about 50 percent saturated fat, including about 40 percent oleic acid, and 10 percent polyunsaturated fatty acids. OxG, the hybrid that produces fera fruit, contains 50 percent oleic acid, 33 percent saturated fatty acids, and 12 percent polyunsaturated fatty acids.

As a dietitian, I can get behind these improvements, but the benefits don't translate to real-world benefits quite as well.

The only way you'll eat fera fruit oil is if you're enjoying pre-made food, most likely fried food, from an establishment using it, as it's not right now available for consumer purchase. And while food fried in fera fruit oil may be slightly nutritionally better than traditional palm oil (which most establishments in the U.S. aren't using anyway), it's still fried food.

This ratio not only contains less saturated fat, but also helps maintain stability over multiple rounds of deep frying compared to other oils. A study presented at the 21st International Oil Palm Conference found that high oleic palm oil lasted more rounds of frying than palm, sunflower, soy, or canola. Because it has less polyunsaturated fat and more monounsaturated and saturated fat, it resists degradation better. This adds up to cost savings, because the oil can be used multiple times, but there's unlikely much of a health advantage. Deep-frying meat and starchy foods in any oil can create harmful compounds, but the link between reusing oil, oil stability, and human health is less clear.

Industry observers note that unrefined high oleic palm oil is rich in antioxidants, including carotenoids and vitamin E. Fera fruit oil is marketed as clean, neutral-tasting, and expeller-pressed, but it offers no guarantee or information on what antioxidants are in the bottle at use or how much.

So while this all sounds great on paper, it's hard to tell how it actually translates into real-world benefits. Is it worth the hype? I'd personally like to see tangible evidence that it does before shelling out extra money for it, and that evidence doesn't seem to exist yet.

Prior to October 15, Erewhon used avocado oil in its fryers. So while there's no arguing that Fera fruit oil has a healthier fatty acid profile than regular palm oil, how does it compare to other fruit oils, like avocado and olive oil, in terms of both health and sustainability?

In a recent development, while olive oil has strong evidence supporting its positive effects on human health, especially heart health, clinical research on the health effects of high-oleic palm oil, like Fera fruit oil, is limited. In one study, 160 participants had either 25 mL of high oleic palm oil or 25 mL of extra virgin olive oil daily for three months. Both groups had similar reductions in total cholesterol and LDL-cholesterol. While these results are promising, the study was small, and more clinical trials are needed to confidently say high oleic palm oil is as beneficial as olive oil.

Avocado oil has a favorable fatty acid profile of 71 percent monounsaturated fatty acids, 13 percent polyunsaturated fatty acids, and 16 percent saturated fatty acids. Fera fruit oil has more saturated fat and less monounsaturated fat, but no head-to-head studies have tested their health effects.

When an elite grocery store like Erewhon switches to a fresh fryer oil, it's easy to assume it's the healthiest choice. But I wouldn't be so quick to jump on board.

Recent findings suggest that after reviewing the research and understanding the food climate we're presently in, where seed oils are viewed as the culprit of all disease and beef tallow is a cure-all, this honestly seems like just another misguided trend. In the context of reality, when you eat an overall healthy and balanced diet, the occasional fried food, whether it's fried in avocado oil, canola oil, or fera fruit oil, will likely have very little impact on your overall health.

Kelsey Kunik, RDN, is a registered dietician and health writer who covers all-things nutrition for Men's Health and Women's Health.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lunar Energy has unveiled a 25-kW home DC fast charger that will do more than just power up your car really fast. Paired with its next-generation home battery system, the Lunar Fast Charger will also let a compatible EV help keep the house running during an outage and potentially earn money by sending electricity back to the grid.

The new battery system will be available to customers in early 2027, with the charger rollout expected in mid-2027.

Lunar says its home DC fast charger can add roughly 100 miles of range in an hour at up to 25 kW. Actual results will depend on the vehicle and charging conditions.

Sources indicate that this is a DC charger, according to Lunar’s product specifications. It connects directly to the DC side of the Lunar Battery, and Lunar says that setup avoids an electrical panel upgrade for the charger. The product page lists CCS and NACS connector support but doesn’t specify which cars will support bidirectional charging.

It has been revealed that that distinction matters. Charging an EV and sending power back are separate capabilities, so buyers will need to check vehicle compatibility before relying on home backup.

With a compatible EV, Lunar claims vehicle-to-home (V2H) charging could extend backup power through a multi-day outage. How long it lasts will depend on the car’s available battery capacity and what’s running in the house.

It has been revealed that vehicle-to-grid (V2G) payments will also depend on the availability of programs. They aren’t an automatic benefit of installing the charger.

The updated Lunar System has a 13.4 kW inverter and uses 5 kWh battery modules. A single tower holds 10–30 kWh, while towers installed side by side can provide up to 300 kWh.

Lunar is also expanding into small businesses, with pad-mounted configurations reaching 1 MWh. Businesses could use the batteries for backup and to reduce demand charges, or fees tied to their highest power draw.

Sources indicate that the system can work with new solar using Lunar Maximizer panel optimizers, existing solar, or no solar at all. Lunar indicates assembly takes place in California, Georgia, Idaho, and Washington, with engineering and R&D in Mountain View, California.

It has been revealed that lunar AI uses electricity prices, weather forecasts, and a property’s energy use to decide when to charge batteries or supply power. Adding the EV gives it another battery to coordinate with rooftop solar and household battery storage.

The company reports that its California customers using Lunar AI saved an additional $338 on average last year compared with a standard battery operating mode.

Lunar’s Gridshare platform already manages more than 150,000 distributed energy devices worldwide. It groups those resources into virtual power plants (VPPs), allowing utilities and other energy providers to call on stored electricity when demand rises and offer customers incentives for participating. It presently operates VPPs in California, Hawaii, and Texas and is expanding in Utah, Nevada, and Fresh Jersey. It also operates in Europe, the UK, and Japan.

In a recent development, lunar hasn’t yet disclosed pricing or named compatible bidirectional EV models. Those are two crucial details homeowners will need before deciding whether this setup makes sense for their driveway.

#5926. Breaking: Underwater internet cables can help save endangered whales

Breaking: Underwater internet cables can help save endangered whales

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the world’s oceans are crisscrossed by thousands of miles of deep sea fiber-optic cables.
  • “This is truly exciting, as this technology enables real-time data access over tens of [miles], and from land,” mentioned Cornell University bioacoustics researcher Léa Bouffaut.
  • According to recent reports, the latest advancements were recently detailed in the journal Methods in Ecology and Evolution, and build on Bouffaut’s previous work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the world’s oceans are crisscrossed by thousands of miles of deep sea fiber-optic cables. This immense infrastructure is the foundation for much of the planet’s international power transmission and telecommunications, but marine biologists say the lines can provide an unexpected conservation benefit. With a bit of creative retooling, the ocean cables can also function as surprisingly good microphones for monitoring endangered whale populations.

“This is truly exciting, as this technology enables real-time data access over tens of [miles], and from land,” mentioned Cornell University bioacoustics researcher Léa Bouffaut.

According to recent reports, the latest advancements were recently detailed in the journal Methods in Ecology and Evolution, and build on Bouffaut’s previous work. In 2022, her team became the first researchers to demonstrate fiber-optic cable monitoring of blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) and fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus). The two species are respectively the largest and second-largest cetaceans, which also means they generate loud, ultra-low frequency vocalizations under 100 hertz. To record their calls, Bouffaut and colleagues utilized a system called distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). The technique works by sending laser pulses through deep sea cables using specialized equipment, which researchers then analyze for miniscule sonic alterations caused by environmental sound waves. After pinpointing blue and fin whale communications, researchers then used the cables’ positions to map the marine mammals’ movements and population distribution.

Sources indicate that following her initial demonstrations, Bouffaut was curious if DAS could also work for other baleen whale species. The odds necessarily weren’t in her team’s favor—smaller species like the bowhead whale (Balaena mysticetus) and critically endangered North Atlantic right whale (Eubalaena glacialis) issue calls at much higher frequencies between about 150 and 300 hertz. Their vocalizations are also less intense and travel shorter distances, making them even more difficult to parse in DAS data.

Recent findings suggest that in the spring, Bouffaut traveled to the town of Utqiaġvik on Alaska’s North Slope to collaborate with the local Indigenous Iñupiat community of whalers. She also partnered with Arctic broadband tech giant Quintillion, who provided access to one of their own deep sea telecommunications cables. Amid terabytes of DAS recordings, Bouffaut eventually achieved another first in her field. She became the first person to confirm bowhead whale vocalizations by harnessing fiber-optic cables.

“Being able to detect bowhead whales on a telecommunication cable is the proof of concept we need to show that DAS can be used to monitor all baleen whales,” explained Bouffaut.

Sources indicate that although the new strategy isn’t sensitive enough to replace dedicated ocean monitoring using underwater microphone arrays, Bouffaut and her colleagues believe DAS could become an invaluable additional tool. It also showcases a way to convert existing infrastructures into multi-use systems.

In a recent development, “The review is also a call to action for scientists, industry partners and regulators to collaborate,” mentioned Bouffaut. “We now have the technical blueprint to turn global undersea infrastructure into a global network for ocean conservation.”.

#5925. Menopause Was a Hushed Conversation—Until Gen X Changed Everything

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1540 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Menopause Was a Hushed Conversation—Until Gen X Changed Everything

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sharon Cancio, 28, didn’t grow up knowing much about menopause.
  • Sources indicate that cancio didn’t start connecting the dots until she came off birth control at 25 and noticed how dramatically her own mood changed around her cycle.
  • Recent findings suggest that these discussions are a far cry from what conversations around menopause used to look like: nonexistent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sharon Cancio, 28, didn’t grow up knowing much about menopause. She didn’t learn anything about it in school, nor from the women in her family. But when she was a teenager, she started noticing her mother’s mood shifting. Around her mid-to-late 40s, “she became much snappier, more easily irritated, and sometimes just seemed angry in a way that felt completely different from the mom I remembered growing up,” she recalls. “I genuinely thought life had simply worn her down.”.

Sources indicate that cancio didn’t start connecting the dots until she came off birth control at 25 and noticed how dramatically her own mood changed around her cycle. Once she realized her mother had entered perimenopause, she went down an internet rabbit hole to learn about it. Women were discussing—in detail—what was happening to their bodies on TikTok and Reddit. Some women were going through menopause early, others were seeking answers for their symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that these discussions are a far cry from what conversations around menopause used to look like: nonexistent. In the past, there wasn’t much education—or even real discussion—on what happens to the female body after 40, forcing women to hustle through hot flashes and mood swings behind closed doors.

In a recent development, but within the last few years, there’s been a shift: Gen X women are the first to go through this hormonal transition in the age of social media—and they’re not afraid to talk about their experiences, notes Gillan Goddard, MD, an endocrinologist and an adjunct assistant professor of medicine at the NYU Langone Hospital. They’re educating an entire generation of younger women in the process. Posts about brain fog, inconsistent sleep patterns, and unfamiliar-feeling bodies have become the first real health literacy that this generation’s daughters, Gen Zers, have gotten about their own hormonal futures. These small conversations have big implications when it comes to learning more about their future health.

Recent findings suggest that the lack of menopause education starts in classrooms: Almost all U.S. states require teenagers to learn about puberty, reproductive health, and sexual disease prevention through sex education classes. But the content and depth of those classes may not favor women’s health: A 2024 study in the Journal of School Health looked at the state of menstrual health education in U.S. K-12 public schools. Researchers analyzed the education standards from each state’s Department of Education site, searching terms like “menstruation,” “menopause,” “period,” “reproduction,” and “puberty.” It found that menstrual health education—especially menopause—is profoundly rare.

There’s also a lack of menopause education in medical schools. Only 31.3 percent of U.S. ob-gyn residency programs include a menopause curriculum, according to a 2023 study in Menopause. The result resembles a serious disconnect: The transition affects nearly half of the population, but the majority of the doctors tasked with treating menopause have received almost no training on how to do it.

Sources indicate that menopause just isn’t prioritized during residency training. Instead, the “focus during training was placed on surgical skills and labor and delivery responsibilities, both considered more urgent and time-consuming,” states Alyssa Dweck, MD, chief medical officer of Bonafide Health and a Menopause Society Certified Practitioner located in Fresh York City. Ob-gyns can earn certifications in (peri)menopause, from organizations including the Menopause Society and Integrative Women’s Health Institute—but they’re not required. Clinicians should have more comprehensive training in medical school and beyond, says Dr. Dweck. But there should also be more funding and resources for women’s health research for treatment options.

When doctors aren’t familiar with menopause, “mood changes, cognitive changes, and body aches are often misunderstood or ignored,” states Dr. Goddard. This can lead to misdiagnoses, and to women not receiving proper treatment for symptoms caused by menopause. This is pretty common: A 2025 survey conducted by health care manufacturer Biote of over 1,000 women ages 30 to 60 in the U.S. found that 39 percent of women have been misdiagnosed and prescribed medication by a provider for conditions like depression.

In a recent development, tikTok and Instagram have filled the menopause education void in the U.S. Conversations about life in menopause have spread awareness about what the condition is actually like, crushing stigmas. This visibility is not only helping younger viewers learn what they can expect later in life—it’s also helping mothers start more health-forward conversations with their daughters.

Milan Parker, 25, has always had open conversations about health with her mom. “She’s always been really honest with me about what she’s going through, even the more personal parts that people sometimes consider taboo,” she claims. But social media increased this dynamic tenfold: Parker’s mother underwent a hysterectomy due to fibroids at 48, which made her enter early menopause. Following the surgery, her mother joined a menopause support group on Facebook. “Seeing that there were women all across the country going through similar things made her more open to talking to me about it,” Parker says.

For instance, Parker’s mom finally explained how debilitating her hot flashes really were. (She’d stopped going on trips with her because she was embarrassed about looking sweaty.) “There were times when I thought maybe my mom just didn’t want to go out with me,” she notes. “I’m really grateful that she made it something we could actually talk about instead of something that had to stay a secret.”.

For daughters, it can be hard to watch their mothers struggle in menopause and not know how to help, but the experience can also help them grow closer. “The emotional experience can be a mix of empathy, grief, anxiety, and closeness,” claims Ashley Peña, LCSW, a clinical social worker and the vice president of outpatient operations at Mission Connection.

Even though Cancio’s mom didn’t tell her when she was going through menopause, the experience helped her gain compassion for her mother and better understand her own body. “As a teenager, I honestly thought she was just becoming grumpy or ‘getting old,’ which I feel terrible admitting now,” she states. “As an adult woman, I have so much more empathy.”.

Having a raw look at what menopause is actually like—whether through a screen or a conversation with their mother—shapes how younger women view aging and how to prepare themselves for what’s ahead. Hearing that they may one day inevitably experience sleepless nights, sudden anger, brain fog, and the loss of identity can be scary, to say the least. But “open conversation about menopause helps women hear the full scope of menopause experiences and how women dealt effectively with their symptoms,” Dr. Goddard notes. It can make the condition sound less scary to younger women.

In fact, growing conversations around menopause can actually inspire younger women to learn about it earlier. “I am seeing patients of all ages, Gen Z included, who have become more inquisitive and engaged in their health overall,” Dr. Dweck claims. Some of her young patients have told her they’ve already started talking to their older relatives about menopause and hormone health. They’re also more open about discussing fertility and egg freezing.

Even though menopause is now common dinner table conversation, the root of the (non-communication) glitch still needs to be fixed. “The only way we normalize talking about women’s health is by talking about it,” Cancio indicates. “Ask questions, stay curious, and don’t be afraid to learn from women who have already been through it.”.

Industry observers note that mothers going through (peri)menopause can have a series of casual conversations about it with their kids. (The earlier, the better.) They can keep the conversation casual and tailored to the child’s developmental age. For instance, moms with children under the age of 13 can briefly mention that they’re “going through a body change.” Then, as the kids get older, they can talk more openly about what they’re experiencing, indicates Dr. Dweck. Encouraging their children to ask questions about menopause can also build empathy and normalize conversations surrounding health.

On the flip side, Parker wants Gen Z women to pay attention to what their mothers are going through, and not wait until the right moment to spark a conversation. “Having those conversations with my mom has made that feel a lot less scary and a lot more human,” she says. “Every stage of life comes sooner than you think, so it’s worth paying attention to your health long before you feel like you have to.”.

Industry observers note that cancio didn’t feel like she could have those conversations with her mom, which is part of what inspired her to start making content around women’s health topics for younger women. “I started thinking about the girl who was sitting at home Googling something because she was too embarrassed to ask her mom, or the girl who thought something was wrong with her because nobody had ever explained that what she was experiencing was normal,” she notes.

Even though the way that Gen Z is learning about menopause isn’t perfect—whether through a viral post or their mother—it’s still a step in the right direction. By doing her part, Cancio hopes to have a completely different relationship with her future daughter “where no topic about her body is off limits and she never feels like she has to search for answers alone.”.

  • BYD even described it as having “an unapologetically boxy profile” that delivers “the imposing, chunky design that finds favour among SUV buyers, yet delivers a contemporary look.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that BYD just got some good news in its Defender-copycat court battle with JLR. After JLR had BYD’s Netherlands offices raided and documents seized, a Dutch court has now handed BYD an early win, ordering JLR to destroy the documents or face a penalty.

After BYD opened orders for the Ti 7 in Europe and the UK in late July, many (including us at Electrek) compared it to the iconic Land Rover Defender, with its boxy, rugged (yet still elegant) SUV design.

BYD even described it as having “an unapologetically boxy profile” that delivers “the imposing, chunky design that finds favour among SUV buyers, yet delivers a contemporary look.”.

In August, authorities on behalf of the British luxury automaker raided BYD’s offices in the Netherlands without prior warning and seized digital records.

On November 11, a Dutch court in The Hague ruled against JLR and ordered the tech giant to destroy the seized documents, which included launch aims and other technical data, so they wouldn’t fall into anyone else’s hands.

JLR must destroy the documents within 24 hours of the ruling or face a fine of €50,000 ($55,000) for every hour it is delayed, with a maximum penalty of up to €500,000 ($553,000).

Within 24 hours of destroying it, JLR must also provide BYD with third-party confirmation that it has been destroyed. The court also rejected the British automaker’s request to pay a €500,000 ($553,000) fine.

According to Autoweek Netherlands, the ruling is based on the fact that JLR doesn’t need the documents, noting that the Ti 7 has not yet been sold in the European Union.

BYD won the ruling, and JLR is prohibited from taking any further legal action under the initial seizure order, but JLR has already begun summary proceedings over the infringement in Rotterdam and The Hague.

JLR claims that the Ti 7 SUV is a “slavish imitation” and infringes on the intellectual property of the Land Rover Defender and that BYD stripped down the Defender to reverse-engineer some of its technology.

According to recent reports, before the raid, BYD claims it fully cooperated with JLR’s requests. BYD’s lawyers called the British automakers’ raid a “fishing expedition” and claimed that “too many files were seized.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Ti 7 is on sale starting at £47,995 ($64,000) in the UK, on the road. That’s over £20,000 ($26,500) less than the plug-in Defender 110, which starts at £71,840 ($95,500) in the UK.

It has a seven-seat arrangement, which BYD said was specifically designed for the European and UK markets.

As the first vehicle in the UK based on its DM-p (Dual Mode performance) powertrain, BYD mentioned the Ti 7 “vastly exceeds the closest competition,” seemingly another jab at the Defender.

"JLR believes BYD stripped down the Defender to reverse engineer some of its technology".

Reverse engineering isn't illegal. Patent infringement is illegal.

Sources indicate that competition strip down each other's product all the time. As long as they don't use the "exact" same technology, it isn't a copy right issue.

The setup uses three electric motors and a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine, delivering a combined 402 hp (408 PS), enabling it to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph in 4.8 seconds.

The engine primarily powers a 35.6 kWh BYD Blade Battery, which provides a pure-electric WLTP driving range of up to 74 miles. In the city, it has an electric range of up to 102 miles.

Available exclusively in the UK in the flagship Excellence AWD trim, BYD claims that the Ti 7 offers “a level of equipment that exceeds anything that its rivals can offer at this price point.”.

We should learn more about the BYD and JLR legal battle soon. Check back for updates, as this story is still ongoing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite both species being bears, black bears (Ursus americanus) typically won’t go to areas that brown bears (Ursus arctos) frequent. For one, brown bears are bigger, at 600 to 900 pounds to the black bear’s average of 90 to 500 pounds.

Despite her large stature (and award-winning butt), a mother bear in Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska named Volverine instantly turned around when she noticed a female brown bear named Bullseye standing right behind her. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded her the 2026 Nope Award for her quick turn away from Bullseye.

“It took a minute for Volverine to notice Bullseye the brown bear standing right behind her, but when she saw, she noted, ‘Nope!’” the rangers write.

Bullseye is a five-year-old brown bear who is known for dark circles around her eyes, and dark brown fur mixed into her blonde coat. And if you are keeping score at home, this is Volverine’s second award this season. She also won the 2026 Big & Beautiful Award for her beautiful bulky body.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are at the moment awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears like Volverine and eight brown bears like Bullseye. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

#5917. Industry News: sonnen’s newly introduced smart breakers help your home battery last longer

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (728 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: sonnen’s newly introduced smart breakers help your home battery last longer

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (728 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A home battery can do more during a blackout if it isn’t busy running nonessential, energy-hungry appliances.
  • The companies revealed today that they’re integrating ADAPT Energy’s controls and Eaton AbleEdge smart breakers into the SOLRITE–sonnen virtual power plant (VPP).
  • The announcement doesn’t specify pricing, how many homes will receive it, or when existing customers can get it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A home battery can do more during a blackout if it isn’t busy running nonessential, energy-hungry appliances. sonnen and SOLRITE Energy are putting that same principle to work for the grid, adding smart breakers that can temporarily switch off selected household loads while batteries help meet electricity demand.

The companies revealed today that they’re integrating ADAPT Energy’s controls and Eaton AbleEdge smart breakers into the SOLRITE–sonnen virtual power plant (VPP). The setup combines sonnenHub with breakers that manage power-hungry equipment, both during outages and when the grid needs help.

The announcement doesn’t specify pricing, how many homes will receive it, or when existing customers can get it.

A VPP connects home batteries into a network so they can work together as a larger energy resource. This addition gives SOLRITE another way to respond: in addition to controlling the batteries, it can reduce the amount of electricity that participating homes use.

sonnen and SOLRITE used the example of a pool pump, as it’s energy-intensive, nonessential, and runs for longer periods. When an event begins, ADAPT temporarily switches off the pool pump while the sonnen battery sends electricity to the grid.

In a recent development, with less battery power going toward the pump, more can flow to the grid. Across participating homes, that gives the VPP more flexibility than relying on battery dispatch alone.

Homeowners have to opt in to that grid participation, and ADAPT will switch off only pre-approved household loads. Joining the VPP program doesn’t give the operator blanket permission to turn off anything in the house.

“Instead of putting the pressure on homeowners to change the way their home is wired, and to manually manipulate loads during an outage, we’re putting intelligence into their energy system, which provides a seamless and automatic backup power experience for their home,” noted Troy Morgan, president of PanTech Design, the developer of ADAPT Energy.

The breakers also tackle a practical problem with home backup: Massive appliances can drain a battery promptly, and the surge of power some equipment needs to start can overload a backup system just as an outage begins.

ADAPT coordinates the smart breakers with the sonnen battery to automatically switch off large loads during backup operation. When grid power returns, it restores them, so homeowners don’t have to go around resetting individual circuits.

It has been revealed that that also gives homeowners more flexibility later. According to the companies, changing which smart-breaker-controlled loads are switched off during an outage doesn’t require rewiring those circuits.

The installation benefit matters, too. Some backup setups require electricians to move selected circuits into a separate panel. This system manages compatible circuits where their breakers already sit, which the companies say reduces installation complexity and inspection work.

Sources indicate that whole-home backup still has limits. Automatically managing large loads helps the available battery capacity go further; it doesn’t mean every appliance can run at once throughout an outage.

Recent findings suggest that SOLRITE finances, builds, and owns residential solar-plus-storage projects through what it calls Virtual Power Plant Agreements, with no upfront cost to homeowners. It indicates it operates in Texas, California, Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Illinois, with more markets planned.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, “Tennis is a whole-body sport,” states sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open.
  • You also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if we told you tennis has been shown to boost heart health, balance, strength, mental acuity, and mood plus add nearly 10 years to your life, you might think we also had a bridge to sell you. But it’s true: Research reveals that even recreational tennis can have a seriously impressive impact on your health—now and for years to come.

In a recent development, “Tennis is a whole-body sport,” states sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open. “It offers cardiovascular benefits, muscle strengthening, flexibility—all the things you need to deal with any physical challenges later in life.”.

You also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr. Colvin adds. In a 2020 study she co-authored, researchers surveyed over 10,000 tennis players, most of them recreational; about 70 percent played just one to three days a week. The players scored higher than the general population on measures such as physical strength, mental and emotional health, and social engagement. “You don't have to be playing at a very high level to get those benefits,” Dr. Colvin indicates.

Sources indicate that and those benefits appear to extend one’s life: When researchers followed 8,577 people for up to 25 years, they found that those who played tennis an average of 103 minutes a week lived 9.7 years longer than their sedentary counterparts. They also lived significantly longer than cyclists (who get an extra 3.7 years), swimmers (3.4 years), and joggers (3.2 years).

Industry observers note that even if you’ve never played tennis before, it’s never too late to start. Keep reading for five reasons to pick up a racket, hit the court, and do your future self a favor.

Tennis involves bursts of high intensity movement—sprinting to the net, running backwards to lob a volley, stopping and then lunging to the opposite side of the court to hit the ball—all of which can do wonders for your cardiovascular health. It boosts heart rate, maximizes your body’s use of oxygen, strengthens heart muscle, improves circulation, and can lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels. As a result, women who play tennis an average two to three hours a week have a 44 percent lower risk of developing cardiovascular disease and a 66 percent lower chance of dying from it.

When you sprint across the court, swing a racquet, or come to a sudden stop, you’re working your leg muscles, core, shoulders, back, and arms—in other words, strengthening nearly every part of the body. A recent study of more than 5,000 women between the ages 63 and 99 found that those who had greater muscle strength lived the longest. And because you’re also supporting your own body weight as you run and land, the sport also helps increase bone density, Dr. Colvin states. Stronger bones mean a lower risk of fractures and osteoporosis in the future, which is what you need if you want to age well.

Sources indicate that tennis requires coordinated movement and muscle control to maintain fluid footwork and smooth, continuous swings. Your core helps make that possible and is key to good balance. Both core strength and balance can help you avoid falls and fractures as you get older. Another part of balance is visuospatial skill—the ability to recognize environmental cues that help you stay upright. Tennis may help sharpen that, too. In a 2022 study, older tennis players who faced a disruption that could throw them off balance were able to react and steady themselves as well as younger players.

Tennis demands intense focus and decision making. “There’s a lot of active thinking going on,” Dr. Colvin states. “You’re making a lot of split-second decisions while you’re playing, plus thinking about the overall strategy of the game. That kind of mental engagement is important as we get older.” According to research, engaging in that kind of quick and strategic thinking while being physically active may be particularly good at promoting neuroplasticity and boosting cognitive function—both of which can stave off the cognitive decline that can come with age.

According to recent reports, studies have found that people who play tennis regularly tend to be less stressed or anxious than people who do lower-intensity exercise. They also report feeling more optimistic, less depressed, and a greater sense of well-being. Like other high-energy sports, tennis may boost mood by prompting the release of brain chemicals such as endorphins, dopamine, and serotonin. It’s also a fun game to play with friends. “The social aspect of tennis is one of its key benefits,” Dr. Colvin says. Numerous studies show that those kinds of community ties are essential for a long, healthy, happier life. With tennis, that’s built into the game.

Children made some of the Middle East’s oldest known clay figures

💡 Key Takeaways
  • About 10,000 years ago, a Neolithic culture in the southern Levant known as the Natufians became some of the first nomadic hunter-gatherers to transition towards agriculture.
  • In a recent development, the Natufians lived in what is now known as the Fertile Crescent between 9,500 and 13,000 BCE.
  • “This shift required diverse tools, skills, and knowledge, different from those needed for the manipulation of stone and bone,” the study’s authors wrote.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

About 10,000 years ago, a Neolithic culture in the southern Levant known as the Natufians became some of the first nomadic hunter-gatherers to transition towards agriculture. But even before this monumental lifestyle shift, members of the prehistoric community were already crafting symbolic figures from clay. What’s more, archaeologists say more than 150 recently discovered artifacts dating back 11,500 to 15,000 years ago are likely the earliest examples of their kind ever found in the Middle East. Their findings, published today in the journal PLOS One, suggest that even children sometimes had a role in creating these miniatures.

In a recent development, the Natufians lived in what is now known as the Fertile Crescent between 9,500 and 13,000 BCE. Pre-agrarian and semi-sedentary, the culture likely preceded the region’s first permanent Neolithic settlements. Although archaeologists previously located small figurines linked to the Natufians made from rocks and bones, these clay artifacts have larger implications. Crafting items from preexisting hard materials typically relies on intentionally shaping through processes like breaking, sanding, or whittling. The existence of clay items suggests that the Natufians didn’t just express themselves artistically and symbolically. They did so through materials that required additional steps like baking and hardening.

“This shift required diverse tools, skills, and knowledge, different from those needed for the manipulation of stone and bone,” the study’s authors wrote.

The figurines found at sites across present-day Israel include depictions of animals like birds and hooved mammals like deer, as well as both male and female individuals. Some of the pieces exhibit traces of pigment and other dyes, while others still feature ancient fingerprints of the artists themselves. Further examinations of these indentations shows that clay sculpting was an intergenerational craft, with both children and adults taking part in the activity.

Recent findings suggest that “Thousands of years before agriculture and pottery emerged, people were already using clay to create figures, as part of their beliefs and knowledge of the natural world,” Laurent Davin, a study co-author and archaeologist at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, remarked in a statement. “What is particularly fascinating is the evidence that children were involved in making these objects, suggesting that creativity and cultural knowledge were shared across generations.”.

Industry observers note that engwe has impressed us repeatedly with its value e-bikes at lower-than-believable prices. But lately, the brand is climbing the value chain with impressive e-bikes that aren’t just great value but also pack strong specs and impressive features. The Engwe M20 3.0 is a great example….

The Engwe M20 3.0 is a specs monster and blows away the original version of the bike released in 2023:.

Recent findings suggest that the M20 is fairly easy to assemble. At just over 100lbs, it is a bit hard to move around, but once assembled, it feels like a pretty impressive piece of machinery. I love the street tires on here instead of pretending to be an off-roader. Dual bright headlights and brake light with turn signals really give this thing some street cred. Adding to the safety roster, Engwe upgraded the quad-piston brakes with sporty red calipers and 202 mm rotors. This is not a value bike. The rear suspension is tight, which is great for 2 riders but might feel stiff out of the box for light riders. The seat is *chef’s kiss* even for 2 riders. Very soft and comfortable but not too soft. It even has a little ‘gas tank’ storage area aft the seat, which is keyed and enough to hold a few sandwiches, some riding gloves, or a small purse.

According to recent reports, one gripe: There are 3 sets of keys on here, the aforementioned storage area and one set each for each battery. We’d love to see these things keyed together.

Industry observers note that the bike/moped/moto came with a huge 1.2 kW battery (or 2 in our case – unless you have a 80-mile commute, 1 should be plenty) that must be charged individually. But with a 60V 8A charger, each one only takes about 2-3 hours to charge, which is impressive.

I did not expect to like the ride of this thing as much as I did. We can dispense with the pleasantries here; it came set to Class 2 mode with a 20mph top speed and stickers to match; a quick Google search will show you how to open this up to 40mph open mode. I take responsibility for my own actions.

It has been revealed that the first thing you’ll notice here is that the motor is whisper-quiet, and with the street tires, there is very little road noise, even at 35mph. The half throttle is plenty responsive, a lot more so than the cadence sensor on the pedals, which are vestigial at best here. Those massive brakes are a bit softer than I’d prefer, but given a good squeeze, those 203mm rotors and quad-piston hydraulic brakes are going to stop you, the 100lb bike, and your passenger/cargo fairly quickly.

In a recent development, my girlfriend and I got pulled over for the first time in my e-biking life as I was picking her up at the coffee shop. The cop was immediately apologetic because “he thought we were kids” and not the 50-year-olds under the helmets he encountered. Then he noticed the pedals and noted that we’re all clear and that what we were on looked like a motorcycle and that a couple of e-moto kids had gotten into accidents recently, one hit by a drunk driver and who is still in a coma. While he was already letting us go, I pointed out the Class 2 sticker on the bike, and he gave me the thumbs-up as we sped off at 30mph. This M20 passed the local police test with flying colors. I can’t guarantee you’ll have the same experience in your jurisdiction.

Most of my gripes on this e-bike are inherent to the form factor. It is heavy at over 100 lbs, but you’d expect that with a 3.3kW motor, 2.4kW of batteries, and room for two. That said, don’t buy this bike if you need to take it up stairs or initiative to pedal it without assist. In fact, this isn’t a bikepath bike or a put it on the back of your car bike. And, don’t buy this bike if you like to pedal. It’s too big and fast. This is a 35 mph roads bike. Also 3 sets of keys?

I did not expect to love this bike as much as I have. It is the perfect train station bike for me, and as a bonus, it is a great way to take my girlfriend to the coffee shop on the weekends. It has fat tires, great suspension, a cushy seat, and strong, smooth acceleration and confidence-inspiring braking. It looks cool enough for the cops to think I’m a kid picking up his girlfriend, and it has so much range that I probably won’t need to charge it monthly. At $1399-$1699 (10% off) depending on battery config, this is less than half the price of some of the pricier and admittedly more stylish Super73 options out there.

Sources indicate that I understand that some will fault Engwe for selling a 3.3kW motor e-bike as a class 2 e-bike. But I genuinely feel safer on the road, being able to go at the 35mph speed that cars are going rather than forcing them to go around me. Plus, it isn’t like every single car on the road goes over the speed limit. So why not bikes too?

The Engwe M20 3.0 is over the limit but in all of the best possible ways.

#5905. There’s No Irony in The Armored League. Only Steel.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2265 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Menshealth ↗ Open Full Page

There’s No Irony in The Armored League. Only Steel.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “THERE’S A LOT more work to do,” Damion DiGrazia muses, as 30 or so individuals spread themselves out across the gymnasium at the Manhattanville Community Center in Harlem.
  • The class does not have a format in the traditional sense.
  • A group forms around the pieces of armor to begin the painstaking process of polishing and assessing each one for damage or repairs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“THERE’S A LOT more work to do,” Damion DiGrazia muses, as 30 or so individuals spread themselves out across the gymnasium at the Manhattanville Community Center in Harlem. A pair of double doors swings lazily back and forth, marking a procession of students and the boxes they carry. DiGrazia leans against the wall, dressed in a red polo and khaki trousers, watching his small community unpack and ready itself for training.

The class does not have a format in the traditional sense. There is no lantern-jawed instructor with a whistle and a clipboard. No snap of uniforms in sync with the rhythm of a kata. There is not even, as far as I could tell, a formal warm-up. Instead, the room seems to have its own sense of internal order.

A group forms around the pieces of armor to begin the painstaking process of polishing and assessing each one for damage or repairs. Some—a breastplate, maybe a set of greaves—are singled out and ferried to a corner, where three individuals sit, cross-legged, and carefully hammer out the dents.

Ropes are thrown over the basketball hoops, and as soon as they land, students appear and begin practicing striking drills with blunted steel weapons. There are, admittedly, a lot of people with weapons. It’s a little surreal at first. When you encounter a fighter in full armor with a sword and buckler or a mace, there is a sense of visual cohesion. It is an entirely different matter to pass a fighter in cutoff denim and a T-shirt practicing elegant, sweeping strikes with an axe.

At the back of the room, the mats find their way into a rectangle, and small scrimmages begin with foam swords and shields. The training takes on its own rhythm; newer members train with foam swords and shields around the edges of the room, while the more seasoned fighters, now sporting what appear to be hockey helmets with face masks, begin grappling practice at its center. Everyone seems to know where they need to be and what they need to do.

In a recent development, it’s taken a long time to get here—years, actually, 13 of them, to be precise. After serving in the military, DiGrazia traces a path through Columbia University, then Harvard, before landing a job at Morgan Stanley. Finding the rhythm of corporate life increasingly dull, he sought relief through extreme sports. DiGrazia started with the classics: marathons, ultramarathons, scuba diving, skydiving, martial arts. But nothing really stuck; he was always chasing something else. That is, until a happy accident. DiGrazia tried what he thought was going to be “full-contact” LARPing (live-action role-playing), but found the experience less than fulfilling: “You couldn't punch people, couldn't grapple people, couldn't kick people, nothing,” DiGrazia notes. The participants were wearing plastic armor, and a hit to the leg saw fighters taking a theatrical knee and swiping at their opponents. At the end of the practice, however, DiGrazia found himself sticking around, commiserating with another fighter, Zorikh, whom he credits as starting his journey along a path that would lead to him founding Gladiators NYC, and laying the groundwork for The Armored League.

Modern armored combat has a longer history in Europe, and DiGrazia found himself bouncing all over the continent, fighting in Poland or next to a castle in Spain. If you wanted to fight in armor, Eastern Europe was where you had to go. Stateside, the early days were decidedly underground and homebrew. Your options were more limited: small groups of fighters met in parking lots and cornfields. Orlando Mendez, one of the founding members of Gladiators NYC, remembers “a lot of horse arenas.” They were one of the few places you could throw someone into a wall without complaint. It was a sport that grew anywhere it could find space. Jason Puerta, owner of Golden Ring Combat, a West Coast armored combat group, recalls regularly fighting on the lawns of a corporate campus after securing the bemused blessing of the local security outfit. It wasn’t quite Fight Club—new members were always welcome (and still are), and people were encouraged to talk about it. Instead, the group could be said to be self-selective: “You either got the hang of it, or you just turned in your armor at the end of the day,” DiGrazia recalls. There were few rules, no weight divisions, and no weapon classes.

In these early years, the attrition rate was high. DiGrazia estimates about half of the participants quit within weeks. Even when he first secured the community center and started spreading the word about classes, he remembers sitting on a bench in the gym, staring at the doors, waiting for someone, anyone, to come to a class. Eventually, they did.

The free classes, access to equipment, loaner armor, and the open exhibition matches in Newly introduced York’s Central Park—all of these, he believes, must remain core elements of the community and the sport. Gladiators NYC also has a nonprofit arm called “Santa’s Knights” where armored knights go door to door during the holidays and deliver presents to children. His commitment to this approach has not come without difficulties. DiGrazia once partnered with a martial arts school whose owner forbade him from sponsoring students who could not afford the $30 class fee. That school closed during COVID.

Technically, the sport can trace its roots back to the 14th century, when knights, foot soldiers, and men-at-arms would practice combat using dull steel weapons and a mixture of soft and plate armor. It was a way to hone their skills in times of peace. The fundamentals of the practice remain in a number of combat sports to this day, but one need only watch a bout of Olympic fencing (or “pointy tag” as Mendez described it) to realize the distance traveled. The Armored League, however, doesn’t seek a return to its medieval origins or even to the stringently historically accurate expressions, which tend to dominate in Europe. When pressed about this, DiGrazia gives an exasperated sigh: “I don't want some librarian walking around looking with a fucking magnifying glass on everybody's goddamn rivet. Leave us alone. Let's have a good time.” The aim is to bring the spectacle and joy to upcoming audiences.

Sources indicate that even if, at first, you cannot follow the scoring, the fights are pure melodrama. Like any combat sport, the fighters’ stats are announced as they enter the ring—with one key distinction: their weight includes their suit of armor. Short of a quirk, it communicates the impact of the sport in a more visceral way: when a pair of combatants crash to the ground or bounce off the chain-link fencing, that’s close to 600 pounds of flesh and steel set in ballistic motion.

Recent findings suggest that bouts are divided into three to five one-minute rounds. Points are awarded based on strikes—where they land and how hard. Basic, clean strikes with weapons, shields, or fists get a base number of points. Meanwhile headshots, two-handed weapon strikes, and slugging a downed opponent get you even more. The bouts are judged by a panel set to one side of the ring, while a pair of counters runs frantically around the perimeter counting strikes.

In a recent development, there are comparatively few rules beyond some basic safety precautions: no stabbing or thrusting; no stomping; no strikes at the inner elbows, armpits, or the backs of knees; no slashing at the neck; and no submissions. Save for these, anything goes, and this adds to the thrill of the fights. Fighters are also not limited to their weapons, and in some cases, they will stand and trade blows like boxers. Though all of the serious fighters have broad and varied martial arts backgrounds—and training approaches—there's a roughly consistent path that leads to The Armored League. Snatches of Muay Thai knee strikes, judo sweeps, classical boxing, escrima, and BJJ are all visible in the blur of limbs, steel, and weapons. One can only imagine how the “librarians” would feel about that.

Sources indicate that strikes may come in flurries or great arcs, but most are hard enough to send sparks flying off the helmets. There is a marshal in the ring with the fighters, notably unarmored save for a yellow flag that’s mainly used to break the fighters up at the end of each round, which frequently ends in a tangle of armor and weapons on the floor of the ring.

It has been revealed that there are two elements that, despite the passage of centuries, have not changed: cost and danger. Historians are divided on the exact conversion rate between 1400 and today, and most put it in terms of wages. They quote the cost of a full set of armor at somewhere between 12 and 18 months of pay. What’s universally agreed upon is that arms and armor were (and remain) anything but cheap. A full suit—then, as now—weighs anywhere from 60 to 80 pounds.

This century, prices start at around $5,000 and climb precipitously with customization. It can take anywhere from a few weeks to a year for delivery. Most participants build their suits over time as they are drawn deeper into the sport.

Building a full set is not easy. A cursory search online will lead you to a number of pages, which might appear to offer armor, but these sites are largely focused on cosplayers or LARPers. That armor will certainly hold together for a walk through Comic-Con, but it will do little to protect from a real blow. The handful of armorers still working today have long wait lists. Puerta notes that despite this, the communal nature of the sport means that much of the armor is passed down or traded between the combatants: as someone upgrades or hangs up their helmet, the armor finds its way into a new pair of hands or onto a new person’s shoulders. At Gladiators NYC, fighters who graduate from the classes, from “softs” (padded armor), and wish to try their hand at the real thing, can borrow pieces from Gladiators NYC’s own armory.

Amongst the current fighters who regularly participate in Armored League matches, almost all fight in custom armor. The suits must adhere to certain safety standards—thickness of steel, comprehensive eye protection, etc. But beyond that, there’s ample room for self-expression.

For example, Abeid “Mando” Mitchell fights in comparatively minimalist and lightweight armor and is readily recognizable by his distinctive helmet, which was made in the style of the Mandalorian from Star Wars. Luke “The Red Knight of Brooklyn” has assembled what he refers to as “a sporting replica” of 1480s armor in keeping with his own, more classical concerns.

According to recent reports, despite the care and attention each fighter devotes to their own armor, at all of the matches I attended, I saw weapons traded freely, shields swapped, even gauntlets lent. For as much violence as there is inside of a 60-second round, there is an equal, if not greater, level of care at the bell. The armor is not just for show; it’s for safety. Combatants want to win as much as they want to ensure their opponent walks off the field under their own power. It’s a fine balance, and as Mendez put it, “once you put on the armor and you get your ass beat a couple of times,” everybody is basically friends.

It has been revealed that nevertheless, it takes a toll. Puerta told me a story of how he almost lost his left eye when the tip of a sword slipped through the bars of his helmet. Others relayed stories of being crushed in a melee and of “helmet terrors” where breathing heavily in the confines of a helmet causes a buildup of carbon dioxide and creates a sensation similar to drowning.

What does the future look like? In my time with the League and Gladiators NYC, I sensed I was watching a sport in its adolescence. It is a league and community that seems to blink in the stark light of its own success and rapidly growing audience. Social media has made it easier for these once disparate communities to connect; the cornfields and horse rinks have been parlayed into an Octagon at the Melrose Ballroom in Queens or a showcase at a theater in Times Square. The bleachers that once held a smattering of friends and family have shifted into crowds drawn from all walks of life—at the sold-out show in Queens, the lines stretched around the block and some people waited an hour just to get into the venue. The Central Park exhibition matches, which happen every second Saturday of the month, have begun to draw crowds that can number over a thousand.

DiGrazia and his merry band have come a long way from the leaner years, when they struggled to find space to practice, the years when they fought in the parking lots of regional hotels in the Midwest or in the summer heat on the boardwalk in Coney Island.

Industry observers note that still, there is, for now, little to no money in this sport. The community, and the fighters too, all have day jobs. They are PhD students, fitness instructors, photographers, and graphic designers. One manages a magic and costume shop. Again, Fight Club springs to mind, as each goes about their day job, bearing the marks of a Thursday brawl or a weekend match, one can only wonder if anyone sees a bruise sticking out of a shirt sleeve and stops to ask just where it came from.

Industry observers note that if you’ve been saving money for Black Friday, there has been a change of intends. Every year, Barnes & Noble slashes prices on Criterion collection movies and box sets by half. It’s the next best thing to being in the Criterion Closet. Most of the bestselling single-film 4K discs in the Criterion sale are $24.99, the bestselling standard Blu-rays are mostly $19.99, and the big director box sets are half off too. B&N ships orders of $60 or more for free, so three of the $24.99 4K discs clear the bar. The discount doesn’t stack with B&N’s Premium Membership discount, and a few of the most popular upcoming 4K releases are already out of stock online. We checked every price and stock status in this post on Barnes & Noble Wednesday afternoon, November 11.

A family movie night pick that holds up for the grown-ups.

Plenty of family movies wear thin for the adults in the room by the fifth viewing, but The Princess Bride keeps getting quoted at dinner tables for a reason. The Criterion edition of The Princess Bride is $24.99 at Barnes & Noble, half of its $49.99 list price. B&N lists it as a 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray combo, so the standard disc covers any player in the house that can’t handle 4K. Rob Reiner’s 1987 fairy tale is a good place to start if you’re building a disc collection for a family that mostly streams.

The Coens’ Best Picture winner on 4K disc.

Sources indicate that javier Bardem’s coin-flipping hitman is one of the scariest villains of the century, and the film around him won Best Picture. The No Country for Old Men 4K Blu-ray is $24.99, down from $49.99. Joel and Ethan Coen’s 2007 West Texas chase also stars Josh Brolin as the hunter who stumbles onto $2 million in drug money and Tommy Lee Jones as the sheriff trying to keep up.

Two Kurosawa samurai classics for $40.

Akira Kurosawa made Yojimbo in 1961 and followed it with Sanjuro a year later, both starring Toshiro Mifune as the same scruffy, sharp-witted ronin. The Yojimbo/Sanjuro 4K Blu-ray set puts both films on 4K for $39.99, which works out to about $20 per movie. If Yojimbo’s plot sounds familiar, that’s because Sergio Leone borrowed it for A Fistful of Dollars. This set pairs well with the Seven Samurai 4K Blu-ray, which is $29.99.

Ten films, 20 discs and more than 25 hours of extras.

Sources indicate that this is the splurge pick in the sale, but per film it costs about the same as the single 4K discs and adds a Blu-ray copy of each movie. The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years is $249.99, half of its $499.99 list price, which comes to $25 per film. Criterion says the set includes ten 4K UHD discs in Dolby Vision HDR, ten Blu-rays and more than 25 hours of special features, running from Bottle Rocket through The French Dispatch. Every film in the set has latest 4K masters supervised and approved by Anderson, according to Criterion.

The Princess Bride, No Country for Old Men and Yojimbo/Sanjuro are covered above. Most of the bestselling single-film 4K discs are $24.99, including Wall-E and David Lynch’s Mulholland Dr. A few older classics, like Citizen Kane, are $29.99. You need a 4K player to watch these discs, and our guide to the best Blu-ray players covers the 4K models worth buying.

Industry observers note that the bestselling standard Blu-rays are mostly $19.99, and they play on any Blu-ray player or game console with a disc drive. The KPop Demon Hunters Blu-ray is $19.99 and the KPop Demon Hunters DVD is $14.99, though its 4K edition is out of stock online. Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite is also $19.99.

The Wes Anderson Archive and Yojimbo/Sanjuro are covered above. Box sets get the same 50 percent cut as single discs, and the substantial director collections are where the dollar savings add up. The 30-disc Ingmar Bergman’s Cinema set is $149.99, and the Essential Fellini set is $124.99.

#5893. Industry News: A wobbly exoplanet vanished—but astronomers aren’t worried
